description: We're building an interactive tool that visualizes how NASA-measured Earth variables temperature, rainfall, vegetation  change over time across regions. Beyond charts, it determines whether these changes are statistically significant, revealing what's changing, where, and how much. Built with Django and real NASA data to make Earth trends clear and meaningful
summary:
We built The Marlene File, an educational detective web app. A student plays an intern trained by Marlene, a 1930s detective. They make a hunch, pick a region and a variable, open a sealed case file, and collect three proofs: the raw yearly readings, the trend, and an honest verdict. A Django API serves real NASA GES DISC data (GPCP and FLDAS), 1990-2020, for the Mediterranean, Nile Delta and Sahel, covering precipitation, evapotranspiration and soil moisture. The student can change the time window and the trend is recalculated live with the Mann-Kendall test. At the end, a treasure box compares all nine cases.
This follows the challenge steps: pick a variable and region, set a time period, examine the time series, and test significance. We show the p-value and say statistically significant or not enough evidence yet, never no trend. Four of nine cases are significant.
It matters because people see trends in the news but rarely learn to tell a real trend from chance. Our app teaches that, and is honest about data limits
details:
The Marlene File is an educational detective game that teaches students how scientists judge whether a change in Earth data is real. The player is an intern trained by Marlene, a 1930s detective. In each case they:

  1. make a hunch about one of three variables: precipitation, actual evapotranspiration or soil moisture;
    • the raw readings: 31 yearly values from 1990 to 2020;
    • the trend: Sen’s slope, with a slider to change the time period;
    • the verdict: the Mann–Kendall test and its p-value.

A result is “Statistically significant” when p is below 0.05. Otherwise it is “Not enough evidence yet”, which is different from “no trend”. After the three regions of a variable, the player compares them side by side. After all nine cases, a final board shows every verdict, a chart comparing the change per decade as a percent of each region’s average, and conclusions written from the data. Our data show 4 significant trends out of 9.

Benefits and intended impact
Students learn the five steps of a data detective (variable, region, time period, time series, significance) by doing them, not by reading about them. The game builds habits that matter well beyond climate:

  • ask whether a pattern is strong enough before believing it;
  • know that results can change with the period you choose;
  • remember that one place does not speak for the whole Earth.

Our aim is that students leave able to read a trend claim critically and to say honestly when the evidence is not enough yet.

How it is creative

  • The detective story makes statistics personal. The player gathers proofs and reaches a verdict, so the p-value becomes the evidence that decides the case.
  • Honesty is part of the game. Five of nine cases end with “not enough evidence yet”, and the time-period slider lets students watch a significant result disappear when the start year moves from 1990 to 1995.
  • The three variables tell one water cycle: water falls as rain, rises into the air, and is kept in the ground. Students see that the same place can give different answers for each.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific accuracy. Every number on screen comes from NASA data through our own API, never typed by hand. We checked all nine results automatically.
    • evapotranspiration and soil moisture are model output;
    • the three Sahel results share the same rainfall, so they are not separate proofs;
    • the Nile Delta model ignores irrigation;
    • with nine tests, one false positive is possible by chance.
  • Simplicity. NASA’s guidance says simple trend tests are enough, so we kept the statistics basic and explained them in plain words.
  • Accessibility and reach. The site runs in any browser with no install, and its charts have text descriptions and hover details.
  • A student budget. We used only a laptop and free services, with no live calls to NASA from the website.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Data: NASA GPCP V3.3 and NASA FLDAS Noah V001 from NASA GES DISC, accessed through Earthdata Cloud OPeNDAP.
  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS.
  • Data and statistics: NumPy, netCDF4, SciPy, pymannkendall.
  • Backend: Django, Django REST Framework, SQLite, Gunicorn, WhiteNoise.
  • Frontend: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with charts drawn in SVG.
  • Design: Figma. Code and hosting: GitHub and Render. Testing: Playwright.
  • Hardware: a student laptop only.
  • AI: Claude
